senses.d: A long, thin, sharp implement usually for piercing as in sewing, embroidery, acupuncture, tattooing, body piercing, medical injections, sutures, etc; or a blunt but otherwise similar implement used for forming loops or knots in crafts such as darning, knitting, tatting, etc.
ex: The seamstress threaded the needle to sew on a button.
reusable needles

senses.d: Any slender, pointed object resembling a needle, such as a pointed crystal, a sharp pinnacle of rock, an obelisk, etc.
A fine measurement indicator on a dial or graph.
ex: a compass needle
The needle on the fuel gauge pointed to empty.

senses.d: A sensor for playing phonograph records, a phonograph stylus.
ex: Ziggy bought some diamond needles for his hi-fi phonograph.

senses.d: A needle-like leaf found on some conifers.
A strong beam resting on props, used as a temporary support during building repairs.
The death penalty carried out by lethal injection.
A text string that is searched for within another string. (see: needle in a haystack)
Any of various species of damselfly of the genus Synlestes, endemic to Australia.
A move in which the performer begins with two hands and one leg on the floor, then kicks the other leg into a full split.
To pierce with a needle, especially for sewing or acupuncture.
ex: Possibly the greatest effect is achieved in the hand by needling the thumb, the index finger and the region of the 1st and 2nd metacarpal.

senses.d: To tease in order to provoke; to poke fun at.
ex: Billy needled his sister incessantly about her pimples.
To needle Lady Leviathan, Hel has convinced her husband to agree to the heartful offer.

senses.d: To form, or be formed, in the shape of a needle.
ex: to needle crystals

ety.text: Inherited from Old French coudre, cosdre, from Vulgar Latin *cōsere, from Latin cōnsuere. The original Old French infinitive was *co(u)sre, where -d- was inserted as a gliding sound. The preconsonantal -s- then became silent, in this case dropping from the spelling relatively early on.

ety.text: From Middle English need, nede, a merger of two terms: * Old English nīed (West Saxon), nēd (Mercian), nēad (“necessity, compulsion, want”), from Proto-West Germanic *naudi, from Proto-Germanic *naudiz, from Proto-Indo-European *neh₂w- (“death”). * Old English nēod (“desire, longing”), from Proto-West Germanic *niudi (“desire, eagerness”), from Proto-Indo-European *new- (“to incline, tend, move, push, nod, wave”).
From Middle English neden, from Old English nēodian.

senses.d: A requirement for something; something needed.
ex: There's no need to speculate; we can easily find out for sure.
She grew irritated with his constant need for attention.

senses.d: A desire or craving for the satisfaction of a requirement perceived as essential or primal.
Lack of means of subsistence; poverty; indigence; destitution.
ex:
Famine is in thy cheeks;
 Need and oppression starveth in thine eyes.

senses.d: To have an absolute requirement for.
ex: Living things need water to survive.
You do not always need to go to the library to study. You may use the Internet.

senses.d: To want strongly; to feel that one must have something.
ex: After ten days of hiking, I needed a shower and a shave.

senses.d: To be obliged or required (to do something).
ex: I need not go if I don't want to, need I?
I was wondering if I need fill in more forms. - No, that's the only one you need fill out.

senses.d: To be required; to be necessary.
ex: When we have done it, we have done our duty, and all that is in our power, and indeed all that needs.

senses.d: To be necessary (to someone).
ex: More ample spirit, then hitherto was wount, / Here needes me […]

grp.label: to have an absolute requirement for
